title: A thoracic cord pattern after trauma

blocks.text: A thoracic cord pattern after trauma

AMaC MRCP PACES · R5-175 · Neurological examination · PACES Station 3, neurological examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 examination, at least 4 questions) · Guideline dates and links in section 15 · Related AMaC: condition may appear elsewhere in a different context

Dear Doctor, examine the legs of a man aged 43, who sustained a thoracic spinal cord injury two years ago. Describe the neurological pattern and discuss further assessment and ongoing care. He uses a wheelchair and cannot stand independently. His spine is stable; do not attempt a standing transfer. An assistant can help with repositioning.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK: A chronic cord injury is demonstrated by upper motor neurone leg signs and a sensory level.
TRAP: Leg power alone cannot establish neurological completeness or an AIS grade; sacral assessment and the full standardised examination are required.

rows: “How do you normally move and position your legs?”
Use assistance, protect skin and respect spasms and joint limits.
“I am checking stiffness, reflexes and the boundary of altered feeling.”
Assess tone, power, reflexes and plantars, then map sensation up the trunk with permission.
“I would need the full spinal injury examination before grading the injury.”
Ask about the documented neurological level and sacral assessment; do not perform an unexpected intimate examination.
“Bladder function, skin and sudden blood-pressure symptoms matter as well as leg movement.”
Review specialist follow-up, continence, pressure care, spasticity, pain and autonomic dysreflexia education.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): tries to stand the patient unsupported.
Uses bed or wheelchair positioning with consent and assistance.
Checks the patient’s usual handling method and protects pressure-sensitive areas.
Calls the chronic legs flaccid without testing.
Finds spastic paraplegia with brisk reflexes and extensor plantars.
Recognises that acute spinal shock would have a different temporal context.
Invents a sensory level from leg findings alone.
Requests permission and maps the trunk.
Describes the observed boundary without confusing vertebral and neurological levels.
Explains the need for sacral sparing and a standardised full assessment for grading.
Links bladder, skin, pain and spasticity care to the patient’s daily routine.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): dismisses sudden headache and sweating.
Recognises possible autonomic dysreflexia as an emergency.
Calls for urgent BP assessment and the spinal-unit emergency pathway while checking triggers.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade.
Skills: A physical examination; B identifying physical signs; C clinical communication; D differential diagnosis; E clinical judgement; F managing patients’ concerns; G maintaining patient welfare.

Patient: a former delivery supervisor, with an established traumatic thoracic cord injury after a road collision. You use a wheelchair and have no useful voluntary leg movement. You manage intermittent catheterisation and a bowel programme taught by the spinal unit. You take prescribed oral baclofen at a stable dose, monitored by the spinal unit. No known drug allergies. Your baseline condition is stable, without current fever, new pain or skin breakdown.

If asked: spasms worsen when the bladder is overfull or you are constipated. Your specialist card warns about autonomic dysreflexia; your injury is recorded at a high thoracic level. Your concern is a return to office work, not a demand for a walking prognosis. Say, “Please ask before moving me; I get spasms.” Permit light-touch and appropriate sensory examination. Any intimate sacral testing is discussed, not unexpectedly enacted on a role-player.

Findings and delivery. Legs show reduced bulk with marked spasticity and adductor spasms. No voluntary movement is demonstrated in the tested leg muscle groups. Knee and ankle reflexes are brisk; ankle clonus and bilateral extensor plantars are present. Truncal sensation is normal through the T5 dermatome and reduced below it on the supplied light-touch/pinprick assessment. Arms and cranial nerves are normal. The old specialist record describes a thoracic injury; sacral sensation and voluntary anal contraction are not supplied here. Therefore neither AIS grade nor completeness can be assigned. No current autonomic episode or new deterioration is present.

Question ladder. Q1 (R4) Where do the signs localise? A chronic thoracic spinal cord syndrome, supported by bilateral leg pyramidal signs and a truncal sensory boundary. Q2 (R4) Is the injury complete? Not established. A full standardised examination including sacral function and review of the record is needed. Q3 (R2) Why are the reflexes brisk? This is a chronic upper motor neurone pattern. Acute cord injury can initially produce reduced tone and reflexes during spinal shock. Q4 (R5) What ongoing care matters? Specialist spinal injury rehabilitation, safe bladder/bowel management, skin surveillance, pain and spasticity care, equipment and meaningful participation goals. Q5 (R6) He suddenly has a pounding headache and sweats above the lesion. What now? Stop the routine examination, sit him upright if feasible, obtain urgent help and repeated BP monitoring, and follow the autonomic dysreflexia pathway. Check reversible triggers such as bladder obstruction and constricting clothing, with trained support; do not leave him waiting.
Handles and positions the patient safely (A G).
Obtains, rather than assumes, a sensory boundary (A B).
Avoids an unsupported completeness classification (D).
Identifies urgent autonomic symptoms and routine rehabilitation priorities separately (E G).
Fail performance
CANDIDATE attempts to stand the patient and declares an AIS A injury because the legs do not move. [R1 Fail R4 Fail] Ignores the dysreflexia card. [R6 Fail]
Pass performance

CANDIDATE demonstrates spastic paraplegia and asks permission to map the trunk. [R2 Pass R3 Pass] “This is a thoracic cord pattern; I cannot grade completeness from the information given.” [R4 Pass] Includes bladder and pressure care. [R5 Pass]
High-performance performance

CANDIDATE uses the patient’s own handling expertise, distinguishes a neurological level from the original bony injury and responds promptly to the hypothetical autonomic event. [R1 High R3 High R6 High] EXAMINER: treats the person as an expert in their routine while retaining responsibility for emergency recognition.
R1: Unsafe transfers lose welfare marks regardless of localisation.
R4: Completeness depends on sacral assessment, not simply paralysis.
R5: A list of complications is less useful than an individual management plan.
“I should ask how you are normally positioned before moving your legs.”
“I have a sensory boundary, but not the full information for an AIS grade.”
“A sudden headache with this injury level needs urgent blood-pressure assessment.”

A thoracic cord lesion can spare arms while producing a spastic leg syndrome, sensory disturbance and sphincter dysfunction. The dermatome identified on bedside testing is not automatically the same as the fractured vertebra. Specialist classification requires a full standardised spinal examination. High thoracic injuries can be complicated by autonomic dysreflexia, which NICE treats as a medical emergency. NICE NG211 supports ongoing multidisciplinary rehabilitation and safe bladder care; NG41 addresses new acute spinal injury, not a standing indication for repeat trauma imaging in a stable chronic case.
THINK: Cord pattern, safe handling, then complications.
SAY: “I cannot determine completeness from the leg examination alone.”
DO: Tone, power, reflexes, plantars and a consented sensory map.
NUMBERS: T5 is the supplied sensory boundary, not an assumed vertebral fracture level.
TRAP: Unsupported standing or an invented AIS grade.
FINISH: Spinal-unit follow-up, participation goals and emergency autonomic awareness.

NICE NG211, Rehabilitation after traumatic injury, 18 January 2022: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng211 — supports spinal injury rehabilitation, bladder/skin care and recognition of autonomic dysreflexia as an emergency. Accessed 17 October 2026.

NICE NG41, Spinal injury: assessment and initial management, 17 February 2016: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng41 — supports the separate pathway for acute/new injury and specialist communication. Accessed 17 October 2026.
